Content:
Suppose we have a quadratic equation like
[MATH: x^2-25 = 0.]
We can solve this equation using the difference of squares formula, shown below:
[MATH: {\color{red}a}^2 - {\color{blue}b}^2 = ({\color{red}a}+{\color{blue}b})({\color{red}a}-{\color{blue}b})]

Content:
Using the difference of squares formula, we can factor the left-hand side of our quadratic equation:
[MATH: x^{2} − 25|= 0; x^{2} − 5^{2}|= 0; (x + 5)(x − 5)|= 0]

Content:
Finally, we apply the zero product rule to get

Content:
[MATH: x+5=0 \qquad\text{or}\qquad x-5=0,]

Content:
which in turn gives

Content:
[MATH: x=-5 \qquad\text{or}\qquad x=5.]

Content:
Therefore, the solutions are [MATH: x=-5,5.] We can write this even more concisely as [MATH: x=\pm 5.]

Content:
Note: We could have solved the equation [MATH: x^2-25=0] using the square root method. However, the factoring method introduced in this lesson will become very useful later when we move on to more complicated quadratic equations. Make sure that you learn it!

sections.normalized_html:
Using the difference of squares formula, we factor the left-hand side of our quadratic equation:

[MATH: a^{2} − 100|= 0; (a)^{2} − (10)^{2}|= 0; (a − 10)(a + 10)|= 0]

Applying the zero product rule, we have

[MATH: a-10=0 \qquad\text{or}\qquad a+10=0,]

which in turn gives

[MATH: a=10 \qquad\text{or}\qquad a=-10.]

Therefore, the solutions are [MATH: a = -10, 10.] We can write this even more concisely as [MATH: a=\pm 10.]

sections.normalized_html:
Using the difference of squares formula, we factor the left-hand side of our quadratic equation:

[MATH: 4z^{2} − 25|= 0; (2z)^{2} − (5)^{2}|= 0; (2z − 5)(2z + 5)|= 0]

Applying the zero product rule, we have

[MATH: 2z-5=0 \qquad\text{or}\qquad 2z+5=0.]

Then, we solve each equation separately:

[MATH: 2z − 5|= 0|2z + 5|= 0; 2z|= 5|2z|= − 5; z|= (5)/(2)|z|= − (5)/(2)]

Therefore, the solutions are [MATH: z = -\dfrac 5 2, \dfrac 5 2.] We can write this even more concisely as [MATH: z=\pm \dfrac 5 2.]

items.title: Solving Perfect Square Quadratic Equations by Reorganizing and Factoring

sections.normalized_html: For which values of [MATH: t] is [MATH: -2t^2 -16 = -5 -3t^2?]
sections.readable_text: For which values of [MATH: t] is [MATH: -2t^2 -16 = -5 -3t^2?]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we move all of the terms to the left-hand side and collect the like terms: [MATH: − 2t^{2} − 16|= − 5 − 3t^{2}; (− 2t^{2} + 3t^{2}) + (− 16 + 5)|= 0; t^{2} − 11|= 0]

Now, using the difference of squares formula, we factor the left-hand side of our quadratic equation:

[MATH: t^{2} − 11|= 0; t^{2} − (sqrt(11))^{2}|= 0; (t − sqrt(11))(t + sqrt(11))|= 0]

Applying the zero product rule, we have

[MATH: t-\sqrt{11}=0 \qquad\text{or}\qquad t+\sqrt{11}=0,]

which in turn gives

[MATH: t=\sqrt{11} \qquad\text{or}\qquad t=-\sqrt{11}.]

Therefore, the solutions are [MATH: t = -\sqrt{11}, \sqrt{11}.] We can write this even more concisely as [MATH: t=\pm \sqrt{11}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we have a quadratic equation like
[MATH: x^2-25 = 0.]
We can solve this equation using the difference of squares formula, shown below:
[MATH: {\color{red}a}^2 - {\color{blue}b}^2 = ({\color{red}a}+{\color{blue}b})({\color{red}a}-{\color{blue}b})]

Content:
Using the difference of squares formula, we can factor the left-hand side of our quadratic equation:
[MATH: x^{2} − 25|= 0; x^{2} − 5^{2}|= 0; (x + 5)(x − 5)|= 0]

Content:
Finally, we apply the zero product rule to get

Content:
[MATH: x+5=0 \qquad\text{or}\qquad x-5=0,]

Content:
which in turn gives

Content:
[MATH: x=-5 \qquad\text{or}\qquad x=5.]

Content:
Therefore, the solutions are [MATH: x=-5,5.] We can write this even more concisely as [MATH: x=\pm 5.]

Content:
Note: We could have solved the equation [MATH: x^2-25=0] using the square root method. However, the factoring method introduced in this lesson will become very useful later when we move on to more complicated quadratic equations. Make sure that you learn it!

Applying the zero product rule, we have

which in turn gives

Therefore, the solutions are [MATH: a = -10, 10.] We can write this even more concisely as [MATH: a=\pm 10.]
